title: Tech Mahindra buys Finastra's cash management software used by banks
subtitle: The Indian IT company used to install these money tools for banks. Now it owns them, along with the team that built them.
content_html:
Picture a mechanic who has fixed the same brand of car for two years. One day, the mechanic buys the whole car design from the maker. That is roughly what happened on Friday, 23 October 2026, when Indian IT company Tech Mahindra said it has bought a set of cash management software products from Finastra, a London software company that works with banks.

Tech Mahindra used to help banks install this software. Now it owns it. The price of the deal was not disclosed.

What exactly did Tech Mahindra buy?

It bought three products, together called a "suite" (a set of tools sold as one family, like a pencil box with a pen, pencil and eraser). According to Tech Mahindra's own press release, they are:

  • Fusion Cash Management (FCM): helps big companies see and move their money through their bank.
  • Fusion Virtual Accounts (FVA): lets one real bank account be split into many labelled "virtual" accounts.
  • Fusion Liquidity Management (FLM): helps track and use the ready cash a company has right now.

The release says Tech Mahindra also got the "IP" behind these products and some related tools. IP means intellectual property. Think of a famous samosa shop. The shop building is one thing, but the secret recipe is the real treasure. Owning the IP means owning the recipe, not just renting it.

The release lists what else came along: tools for payables (money a company must pay), receivables (money a company should get), balance and transaction reports, cash flow forecasting and APIs. An API is like a waiter who carries orders between two kitchens, so two computer systems can talk to each other.

Cash management, explained with a chai stall

Imagine a chai stall owner. Every evening, the owner counts the money in the cash box, checks who still owes money, and keeps aside enough to buy milk and sugar tomorrow. That is cash management.

Now imagine a huge company with thousands of buyers and suppliers in many countries. It cannot count notes in a box. It needs its bank to show, live on a screen, how much money came in, how much went out, and how much is left. Banks buy software like the Finastra suite to give their big business clients this view.

Tech Mahindra's release says corporate banks now care a lot about real-time cash visibility, automatic payables and receivables, following the rules, and lower complexity. Real-time simply means "right now", like a live cricket score instead of tomorrow's newspaper.

Virtual accounts: envelopes inside one wallet

Suppose a student keeps all pocket money in one wallet, but uses small envelopes inside it: one for food, one for travel, one for books. The money is in one place, but it is easy to see what each part is for.

Virtual accounts work the same way for companies. A firm has one real account at the bank, but many virtual ones inside it, maybe one per customer or per city. When money arrives, it is easy to tell who paid. This is one of the three products Tech Mahindra now owns.

From helper to owner

This deal did not come out of nowhere. In August 2024, the two companies signed a partnership. Under it, Tech Mahindra became Finastra's exclusive global implementation partner for its Cash Management platform.

An implementation partner is the team that sets up software for a client, a bit like the electrician who fits and wires a new air conditioner that someone else made. "Exclusive" meant Tech Mahindra was the only such partner worldwide for that platform.

So Tech Mahindra already knew this software well. Finastra said as much. Ruchir Purwar, Finastra's head of partnerships and cross selling sales, said Tech Mahindra "already knows our business well", as quoted by Business Standard.

What happens to the banks already using it?

For a bank, losing the software behind its money tools would be like a school losing its exam app the night before the exam.

The press release says the deal aims to keep things smooth for existing customers, with continued access to the platform, ongoing services and customer support. It also says experienced product engineering and customer success staff move to Tech Mahindra. In simple words, many of the people who built and looked after these products now work for their new owner.

Who are the two companies?

Tech Mahindra is part of the Mahindra Group. Its release says it has more than 150,000 professionals across 90 countries. It does consulting, IT services, cloud work, AI and much more for companies around the world.

Finastra is a British financial software company based in London. It was formed in 2017 by joining two older companies, Misys from London and D+H from Canada. It sells software for retail banking, lending and more. Tech Mahindra's release describes Finastra as software that powers thousands of financial institutions in more than 100 countries, and notes that it is backed by Vista Equity Partners, an investment firm.

Why would an IT company want to own products?

An IT company can earn in two ways. It can sell services, where its people work on a client's project, like a tailor who stitches a suit to order. Or it can own a product. It is like a shop that sells ready-made shirts. Once the design is made, it can be sold again and again.

Tech Mahindra's release says the deal creates an "IP-led platform" for growth in cash management, liquidity management, virtual accounts, supply chain finance, cash flow forecasting and other transaction banking areas. Transaction banking is the everyday money-moving side of banking for businesses: paying, collecting and keeping track.

Anil Venuturupalli, who leads Tech Mahindra's banking products as senior vice president and chief product officer, financial services, said the deal strengthens its banking products portfolio and helps it support financial institutions with cash and liquidity needs, according to the company's release.

What this means for a young reader

If you are studying computer science, commerce or finance, this is a peek at a quiet but huge corner of business. Big companies collect money, pay bills and plan their cash through tools like these, offered by their banks. Few people ever see them.

It is also a simple story of a helper becoming an owner. An Indian IT company that used to install a London company's product has bought the recipe itself.
